blocks.en: "For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails anything, but faith working through love." — Galatians 5:6 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Porque en Cristo Jesús ni la circuncisión vale algo, ni la incircuncisión, sino la fe que obra por el amor." — Gálatas 5:6 (RVG)

blocks.en: The Tree of Faith
blocks.es_reference: El Árbol de la Fe

blocks.en: The root is Christ alone; faith is the trunk; the fruit proves the life.
blocks.es_reference: La raíz es Cristo solo; la fe es el tronco; el fruto prueba la vida.

blocks.en: Texts: Galatians 2:16, 21; 5:6, 22-23; Ephesians 2:8-9; James 2:17, 26
blocks.es_reference: Textos: Gálatas 2:16, 21; 5:6, 22-23; Efesios 2:8-9; Santiago 2:17, 26 (RVG)

blocks.en: "For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast." — Ephesians 2:8-9 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Porque por gracia sois salvos por medio de la fe; y esto no de vosotros, pues es don de Dios; no por obras, para que nadie se gloríe." — Efesios 2:8-9 (RVG)

blocks.en: Grace: The Free Gift of God
blocks.es_reference: La Gracia: El Don Gratuito de Dios

blocks.en: Grace is the beating heart of the gospel, and of this whole letter. To say we are saved by grace is to say that salvation is a free gift — unearned, undeserved, and beyond our power to repay. We do nothing to merit it; we bring nothing to purchase it. As Paul writes, it is "the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast." And he adds elsewhere, "if by grace, then it is no longer of works; otherwise grace is no longer grace" (Romans 11:6). Grace and earning are opposites. The moment we add our own work as a ground of acceptance, we have left grace behind — which is exactly the danger Paul fought in Galatia: "I do not set aside the grace of God" (Galatians 2:21). All that a sinner can do is open an empty hand and receive what God freely gives.
blocks.es_reference: La gracia es el corazón palpitante del evangelio, y de toda esta carta. Decir que somos salvos por gracia es decir que la salvación es un don gratuito — no ganado, no merecido, y que no podemos pagar. No hacemos nada para merecerla; no traemos nada para comprarla. Como escribe Pablo, es "don de Dios; no por obras, para que nadie se gloríe." Y añade en otro lugar: "si por gracia, entonces no es por obras; de otra manera la gracia ya no es gracia" (Romanos 11:6). La gracia y el ganar son opuestos. En el momento en que añadimos nuestra propia obra como fundamento de aceptación, hemos dejado atrás la gracia — que es justamente el peligro que Pablo combatió en Galacia: "No desecho la gracia de Dios" (Gálatas 2:21). Todo lo que un pecador puede hacer es abrir una mano vacía y recibir lo que Dios da gratuitamente.

blocks.en: The Root: Christ Alone
blocks.es_reference: La Raíz: Cristo Solo

blocks.en: Picture the Christian life as a tree. At the root, hidden beneath the soil and bearing the whole weight of the tree, is Christ alone. He is the source of all life in the believer. Our salvation does not rest partly on Christ and partly on us; it rests on Christ wholly. "I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me" (Galatians 2:20). Everything the tree is, and everything it produces, flows up from that one root. Take Christ away and the tree dies; add anything beside Him at the root and you have a different tree — a different gospel. This is why the apostle will allow nothing — not the law, not circumcision, not human merit — to share the place that belongs to Christ alone.
blocks.es_reference: Imagine la vida cristiana como un árbol. En la raíz, escondida bajo la tierra y sosteniendo todo el peso del árbol, está Cristo solo. Él es la fuente de toda vida en el creyente. Nuestra salvación no descansa en parte sobre Cristo y en parte sobre nosotros; descansa enteramente sobre Cristo. "Con Cristo estoy juntamente crucificado; y vivo, no ya yo, mas vive Cristo en mí" (Gálatas 2:20). Todo lo que el árbol es, y todo lo que produce, sube desde esa única raíz. Quite a Cristo y el árbol muere; añada cualquier cosa junto a Él en la raíz y tiene un árbol diferente — un evangelio diferente. Por eso el apóstol no permitirá que nada — ni la ley, ni la circuncisión, ni el mérito humano — comparta el lugar que pertenece a Cristo solo.

blocks.en: Faith: The Empty Hand That Receives
blocks.es_reference: La Fe: La Mano Vacía que Recibe

blocks.en: If grace is the gift and Christ is the root, then faith is the empty hand that receives. Faith is not a work we perform to earn God's favor; it is the very opposite of working. Faith looks away from self and rests entirely on Christ. This is why Paul can say a man is "not justified by the works of the law but by faith in Jesus Christ" (Galatians 2:16). Faith adds nothing to the gift; it simply takes hold of it. A beggar who receives bread does not earn the bread by reaching out his hand. So the believer contributes nothing to his justification but the empty hand of faith — and even that faith is itself a gift of God.
blocks.es_reference: Si la gracia es el don y Cristo es la raíz, entonces la fe es la mano vacía que recibe. La fe no es una obra que realizamos para ganar el favor de Dios; es justamente lo contrario de obrar. La fe aparta la mirada de sí misma y descansa enteramente en Cristo. Por eso Pablo puede decir que el hombre "no es justificado por las obras de la ley, sino por la fe de Jesucristo" (Gálatas 2:16). La fe no añade nada al don; simplemente lo toma. Un mendigo que recibe pan no gana el pan por extender la mano. Así que el creyente no aporta nada a su justificación sino la mano vacía de la fe — y aun esa fe es ella misma un don de Dios.

blocks.en: Did Paul and James Disagree?
blocks.es_reference: ¿Discreparon Pablo y Santiago?

blocks.en: Here many sincere readers stumble. Paul says plainly, "a man is justified by faith apart from the deeds of the law" (Romans 3:28). But James seems to say the opposite: "a man is justified by works, and not by faith only" (James 2:24). Some have claimed the two apostles preached different gospels. They did not. The key is to see that they are answering different questions, and looking at different parts of the same tree.
blocks.es_reference: Aquí tropiezan muchos lectores sinceros. Pablo dice claramente: "el hombre es justificado por fe sin las obras de la ley" (Romanos 3:28). Pero Santiago parece decir lo opuesto: "el hombre es justificado por las obras, y no solamente por la fe" (Santiago 2:24). Algunos han afirmado que los dos apóstoles predicaron evangelios diferentes. No lo hicieron. La clave es ver que están respondiendo preguntas diferentes, y mirando partes diferentes del mismo árbol.

blocks.en: Two Men, One Tree: The Root and the Fruit
blocks.es_reference: Dos Hombres, Un Árbol: La Raíz y el Fruto

blocks.en: Paul looks at the root. His question is, "How is a sinner made right with God?" His answer: by grace, through faith, in Christ alone, with no works added. That happens out of sight, at the root, before God. James looks at the fruit. His question is, "How do we know a person's faith is real?" His answer: by what it produces. That is seen above the ground, before men. Paul uses the word "justified" to mean declared righteous before God; James uses it to mean shown to be righteous by the evidence of a changed life. There is no contradiction here, any more than there is a contradiction between the hidden root that gives a tree its life and the visible fruit that proves the tree is alive. The fruit does not make the tree alive; it shows that it already is.
blocks.es_reference: Pablo mira la raíz. Su pregunta es: "¿Cómo es hecho justo un pecador delante de Dios?" Su respuesta: por gracia, mediante la fe, en Cristo solo, sin obras añadidas. Eso sucede fuera de la vista, en la raíz, delante de Dios. Santiago mira el fruto. Su pregunta es: "¿Cómo sabemos que la fe de una persona es real?" Su respuesta: por lo que produce. Eso se ve sobre la tierra, delante de los hombres. Pablo usa la palabra "justificado" para decir declarado justo delante de Dios; Santiago la usa para decir mostrado ser justo por la evidencia de una vida cambiada. No hay contradicción aquí, como tampoco la hay entre la raíz escondida que da vida al árbol y el fruto visible que prueba que el árbol está vivo. El fruto no hace vivo al árbol; muestra que ya lo está.

blocks.en: Faith Without Works Is Dead
blocks.es_reference: La Fe sin Obras es Muerta

blocks.en: This is exactly James's point: "faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead" (James 2:17); "as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also" (James 2:26). A tree that never puts out a single leaf or fruit, year after year, is not a living tree at rest; it is a dead tree. So a "faith" that produces no love, no obedience, no change is not living faith at all — it is a corpse. James is not adding works to the root as a price for salvation; he is saying that living faith, by its very nature, bears fruit. Where the root is real, fruit will come.
blocks.es_reference: Este es justamente el punto de Santiago: "la fe, si no tiene obras, es muerta en sí misma" (Santiago 2:17); "como el cuerpo sin el espíritu está muerto, así también la fe sin obras está muerta" (Santiago 2:26). Un árbol que nunca echa una sola hoja ni fruto, año tras año, no es un árbol vivo en reposo; es un árbol muerto. Así que una "fe" que no produce amor, ni obediencia, ni cambio no es fe viva en absoluto — es un cadáver. Santiago no está añadiendo obras a la raíz como precio de la salvación; está diciendo que la fe viva, por su misma naturaleza, lleva fruto. Donde la raíz es real, el fruto vendrá.

blocks.en: Faith Working Through Love
blocks.es_reference: La Fe que Obra por el Amor

blocks.en: Galatians itself holds the root and the fruit together, so we need not go outside this letter to reconcile Paul and James. Paul writes that what counts is "faith working through love" (Galatians 5:6) — faith that is alive and active. And he describes the fruit the Spirit grows: "love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control" (Galatians 5:22-23). Notice who produces it: the Holy Spirit, dwelling in the believer who is joined to Christ. The same grace that saves us also sends the Spirit, who bears His fruit through us. Paul fully expects the tree of grace to be heavy with fruit. On this, he and James are entirely one.
blocks.es_reference: Gálatas mismo sostiene juntos la raíz y el fruto, de modo que no necesitamos salir de esta carta para reconciliar a Pablo y a Santiago. Pablo escribe que lo que vale es "la fe que obra por el amor" (Gálatas 5:6) — fe que está viva y activa. Y describe el fruto que el Espíritu hace crecer: "amor, gozo, paz, paciencia, benignidad, bondad, fe, mansedumbre, templanza" (Gálatas 5:22-23). Note quién lo produce: el Espíritu Santo, morando en el creyente que está unido a Cristo. La misma gracia que nos salva también envía al Espíritu, que lleva su fruto a través de nosotros. Pablo espera plenamente que el árbol de la gracia esté cargado de fruto. En esto, él y Santiago son enteramente uno.

blocks.en: Why This Matters
blocks.es_reference: Por Qué Esto Importa

blocks.en: Holding the whole of grace — root and fruit — guards us from two deadly errors. The first is to tamper with the root: to add law, works, or human merit to Christ as a ground of salvation. That is the error of every false gospel, and it is what Paul calls "another gospel" under God's curse (Galatians 1:8-9). The second is to claim the root while bearing no fruit: a dead, empty profession that has never changed the life. The true gospel answers both. We are saved by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone — we do nothing to earn it. And that saving grace is never barren; in time it always bears the fruit of the Spirit. This is the measure by which we will weigh other gospels in the units to come: do they leave Christ alone at the root, and grace as a free gift? Where that root is changed, the gospel itself is lost.
blocks.es_reference: Sostener la plenitud de la gracia — raíz y fruto — nos guarda de dos errores mortales. El primero es alterar la raíz: añadir ley, obras o mérito humano a Cristo como fundamento de la salvación. Ese es el error de todo falso evangelio, y es lo que Pablo llama "otro evangelio" bajo la maldición de Dios (Gálatas 1:8-9). El segundo es reclamar la raíz sin llevar fruto: una profesión muerta y vacía que nunca ha cambiado la vida. El verdadero evangelio responde a ambos. Somos salvos por gracia sola, mediante la fe sola, en Cristo solo — no hacemos nada para ganarla. Y esa gracia salvadora nunca es estéril; a su tiempo siempre lleva el fruto del Espíritu. Esta es la medida con que pesaremos otros evangelios en las unidades que vienen: ¿dejan a Cristo solo en la raíz, y la gracia como don gratuito? Donde esa raíz es cambiada, el evangelio mismo se pierde.

blocks.en: "I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me; and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave Himself for me." — Galatians 2:20 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Con Cristo estoy juntamente crucificado; y vivo, no ya yo, mas vive Cristo en mí; y lo que ahora vivo en la carne, lo vivo en la fe del Hijo de Dios, el cual me amó, y se entregó a sí mismo por mí." — Gálatas 2:20 (RVG)

fill.prompt: By grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the ____ of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast.
Grace and earning are ____; adding our own work as a ground of acceptance leaves grace behind.
Picturing the Christian life as a tree, the root that bears the whole weight of the tree is ____ alone.
In the picture of the tree of faith, the root is Christ alone and faith is the ____.
Faith is not a work that earns God's favor; it is the empty ____ that receives the gift.
Paul looks at the root, asking how a sinner is made right with God; James looks at the ____, asking how we know faith is real.
Paul uses the word "justified" to mean ____ righteous before God.
James writes that faith by itself, if it does not have works, is ____.

sa.prompt: Define grace, and explain why grace and earning are opposites.
sa.model: Grace is the free, unmerited favor of God; to be saved by grace means salvation is a free gift, not something we earn or deserve. Paul says it is the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast. Grace and earning are opposites: Romans 11:6 says that if salvation is by grace, it is no longer of works, or else grace would no longer be grace. The moment we add our own merit as a ground of acceptance, we leave grace behind. A sinner can do nothing to purchase salvation; all he can do is open an empty hand and receive what God gives in Christ. There is no room for boasting, because the whole gift rests on Christ and not on us.

sa.prompt: Explain the tree analogy: what do the root, the trunk of faith, and the fruit each represent?
sa.model: In the analogy the Christian life is a tree. The root, hidden beneath the soil and bearing the whole weight, is Christ alone; He is the source of all life, and our salvation rests wholly on Him by grace. The trunk is faith, the empty hand that receives Christ and unites us to Him. The branches and fruit are the visible result: the fruit of the Spirit and good works that grow up out of the root. The fruit does not make the tree alive; it proves the tree is alive. So grace and Christ are at the root, faith is the trunk, and the fruit is the evidence above ground. Paul looks chiefly at the root; James looks at the fruit; both describe one living tree.

sa.prompt: Why is faith not a work? Use the picture of the empty hand.
sa.model: Faith is not a work because it is the very opposite of working; it earns nothing and adds nothing. Faith is the empty hand that simply receives the gift God gives in Christ. Paul says a man is not justified by the works of the law but by faith in Jesus Christ, which means faith looks away from self and rests entirely on Christ. A beggar who receives bread does not earn the bread by reaching out his hand; the hand only takes what is freely given. In the same way the believer contributes nothing to his justification but the empty hand of faith, and even that faith is itself a gift of God. So to be saved by faith is still to be saved by grace, not by works.

sa.prompt: State the Paul-and-James objection and resolve it, including the two meanings of 'justified.'
sa.model: The objection is that Paul says a man is justified by faith apart from works, while James says a man is justified by works and not by faith only — so they seem to contradict. The resolution is that they answer different questions and look at different parts of the tree. Paul looks at the root and asks how a sinner is made right with God: by grace through faith in Christ alone. He uses justified to mean declared righteous before God. James looks at the fruit and asks how we know a faith is real: by what it produces. He uses justified to mean shown to be righteous before men. There is no contradiction, because the hidden root gives life and the visible fruit proves it; the fruit does not earn the life. Both apostles teach one gospel.

sa.prompt: Explain 'faith without works is dead' (James) without making works the ground of salvation.
sa.model: James says that faith by itself, if it has no works, is dead, like a body without the spirit. His point is not that works are the ground of salvation; the ground is Christ received by faith. His point is that living faith, by its very nature, produces fruit. A tree that never bears a single leaf or fruit is not a living tree at rest but a dead one. In the same way a faith that produces no love, obedience, or change is not living faith at all. So the works are not the price that buys salvation; they are the evidence that the faith is alive. Where the root is real, fruit will surely come; and where there is no fruit, there was never living faith.

sa.prompt: How does Galatians itself hold the root and the fruit together (5:6; 5:22-23; the Spirit)?
sa.model: Galatians holds the root and the fruit together, so we need not leave the letter to reconcile Paul and James. Paul says what counts is faith working through love, which is faith that is alive and active, not idle. He then names the fruit the Spirit grows: love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Notice who produces this fruit: the Holy Spirit, dwelling in the believer who is joined to Christ. The same grace that saves us sends the Spirit, who bears His fruit through us. So Paul himself fully expects the tree of grace to be heavy with fruit. On this Paul and James are entirely one: living faith works through love and bears the fruit of the Spirit.

sa.prompt: What two deadly errors does holding the whole of grace guard against?
sa.model: Holding the whole of grace, root and fruit, guards us from two deadly errors. The first is to tamper with the root by adding law, works, or human merit to Christ as a ground of salvation. That is the error of every false gospel, which Paul calls another gospel under God's curse. The second is to claim the root while bearing no fruit: a dead, empty profession that has never changed the life. The true gospel answers both. We are saved by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone, doing nothing to earn it; and that saving grace is never barren but in time always bears the fruit of the Spirit. Guarding the root keeps us from legalism, and expecting the fruit keeps us from a dead faith.

sa.prompt: Why does adding anything to Christ at the root produce 'another gospel' (Galatians 1:8-9; 2:21)?
sa.model: Adding anything to Christ at the root produces another gospel because the gospel is that we are saved by grace, through faith, in Christ alone. To add law, works, or human merit as a ground of salvation is to change the root, and a tree with a changed root is a different tree. Paul says that if righteousness came through the law, then Christ died in vain, so to add the law is to empty the cross and set aside the grace of God. Because this strikes at the very heart of salvation, Paul pronounces a curse on any other gospel, even from an angel. It is not a small difference but a matter of whether the gospel is kept or lost. Where Christ alone is no longer the whole root, the good news is destroyed.

sa.prompt: What is the Holy Spirit's role in producing fruit, and how does that show Paul and James agree?
sa.model: The Holy Spirit is the one who produces the fruit in the believer. When a sinner is joined to Christ by faith, the same grace that saves him also gives the Spirit, who dwells in him and grows the fruit: love, joy, peace, and the rest. The believer does not manufacture this fruit by willpower; it is the Spirit's work flowing from the root. This shows that Paul and James agree. Paul, who teaches justification by faith apart from works, also says faith works through love and expects the Spirit's fruit. James says living faith produces works. Both are describing what the Spirit does in a person truly joined to Christ. So the doctrine of grace and the demand for fruit are not rivals; the same Spirit secures both.

sa.prompt: Summarize Unit 8: the whole of grace, root and fruit, and the test it gives for weighing other gospels.
sa.model: Unit 8 teaches the whole of grace as one tree, root and fruit. At the root is Christ alone; salvation is a free gift of grace, received by the empty hand of faith, and we do nothing to earn it. The fruit of the Spirit and good works grow up from that root and prove that the faith is alive, though they never make it alive. So Paul, who looks at the root, and James, who looks at the fruit, fully agree. This gives us a clear test for weighing other gospels: do they keep Christ alone at the root and grace as a free gift, and does the Spirit bear real fruit? Where the root is changed by adding works or merit, the gospel itself is lost, and where there is no fruit, the faith was never living. Grace alone, faith alone, Christ alone, bearing the fruit of the Spirit.
